brief: Intro to remote-onboarding guide; company onboarded 27 remote hires in one year; time-to-first-PR cut from 12 days to 5.
facts: Company onboarded 27 remote hires in one year
draft:
Remote onboarding is one of those things every company claims to have figured out — until a new hire spends their first week waiting for access, hunting for documentation, and wondering who to ask for help. In a distributed team, the small frictions of onboarding don't just add up; they compound.

Over the past year, we onboarded 27 remote hires. Along the way, we made plenty of mistakes, ran plenty of experiments, and learned what actually moves the needle. The result? We cut our time-to-first-PR from 12 days to just 5 — meaning new engineers are shipping meaningful code in their first week instead of their third.

In this guide, we'll share the exact playbook that got us there: how we structure the first day, the role of onboarding buddies, the documentation that matters (and the documentation that doesn't), and the metrics we track to keep improving.

Whether you're onboarding your first remote hire or your fiftieth, we hope these lessons help you build a smoother, faster, and more welcoming experience for every new teammate. Because great onboarding isn't just an HR checkbox — it's your first, best chance to show new hires how your team really works. Let's dive in.

brief: Intro to "The State of Design Systems 2026" report; survey of 412 designers; 61% say their design system is partially adopted at best.
facts: 61% say their design system is partially adopted at best
draft:
Design systems have become a cornerstone of modern product development — but how are they actually faring inside organizations? To find out, we surveyed 412 designers across industries, company sizes, and levels of design maturity for The State of Design Systems 2026.

The headline finding is a sobering one: 61% of respondents say their design system is partially adopted at best. In other words, for the majority of teams, the design system exists — but it isn't yet the single source of truth it was meant to be.

Why does adoption stall? The reasons are varied: unclear ownership, competing priorities, gaps between design and code, and the ever-present challenge of keeping documentation up to date. But the data also points to what's working — and the teams that get adoption right share some surprisingly consistent habits.

In this report, we'll unpack the numbers, highlight the trends shaping design systems in 2026, and share practical takeaways you can bring back to your own team. Whether you're just launching your first component library or scaling a mature system across dozens of products, there's something here for you. Let's take a closer look at what the data tells us.

brief: Personal-finance post on emergency funds; recommends 3–6 months of expenses; author built theirs in 14 months on a $52k salary.
facts: Author built their emergency fund in 14 months
draft:
Let's be honest: building an emergency fund isn't glamorous. There's no dopamine hit, no compounding chart to admire, no one bragging about their savings account at parties. And yet, if there's one financial move that consistently pays off, it's this one.

The standard advice is to set aside 3–6 months of expenses — enough of a cushion to absorb a job loss, a medical bill, or a surprise car repair without reaching for a credit card. It sounds simple. It's also, for most people, genuinely hard.

I know because I've done it. It took me 14 months to build my emergency fund on a $52k salary, and along the way I learned that the challenge is less about math and more about habits, trade-offs, and staying motivated when progress feels painfully slow.

In this post, I'll share exactly how I did it: the budget changes that mattered most, the automation that kept me consistent, and the mindset shifts that made all the difference. If you've been putting off starting your emergency fund — or you've started and stalled — I hope this gives you a realistic roadmap, and the nudge to begin today. Future you will thank you.

brief: Travel post on 4 days in Kyoto; stayed in Gion; highlights Fushimi Inari at 6am and a kaiseki dinner that cost ¥18,000.
draft:
There's something magical about Kyoto. The ancient temples, the quiet lanes, the sense that every corner holds a thousand years of history — it's a city that rewards slowing down, even when you only have four days.

That's exactly what we had: four days to soak in as much of Kyoto as possible. We based ourselves in Gion, the city's famous geisha district, where wooden machiya houses and lantern-lit streets make even a simple evening stroll feel like stepping back in time.

The highlights? Walking beneath the vermilion gates of Fushimi Inari at 6am, before the crowds arrived, with the mountain path almost entirely to ourselves. And on our final night, a kaiseki dinner that cost ¥18,000 — not cheap, but an unforgettable procession of seasonal dishes that felt more like art than food.

In this post, I'll walk you through our full four-day itinerary: where we stayed, what we ate, what we'd happily skip next time, and the small tips that made the trip smoother. Whether it's your first visit to Kyoto or your fifth, I hope this guide helps you plan an unforgettable adventure of your own. Let's get into it.

Every week, I see another "revolutionary AI agent" launch. And every week, the pattern is the same: a clever prompt, a polished UI, and a foundation model doing all the heavy lifting underneath.

brief: Career advice: 10 years in B2B sales; the #1 skill is listening; a deal was once saved by shutting up for 90 seconds on a call.
facts: deal saved by staying silent for 90 seconds on a call
draft:
10 years in B2B sales taught me many things.

But the #1 skill? It's not pitching. It's not negotiating. It's not objection handling.

It's listening.

Let me tell you a story. A few years ago, I was on a call with a deal that was falling apart. The prospect had concerns, and every instinct told me to jump in with answers.

Instead, I did something that felt terrifying: I shut up. For 90 full seconds.

The silence was excruciating. But in that silence, the prospect talked themselves through their own objection — and revealed the real blocker, one I never would have guessed.

We closed the deal two weeks later.

Here's what a decade in sales has taught me:
🎧 Prospects will tell you exactly how to sell to them — if you let them
🎧 Silence isn't awkward. It's powerful.
🎧 The best discovery question is sometimes no question at all

Talk less. Sell more.

brief: Failure story: founder shut down startup "Cartful" after 3 years; raised $1.1M; grew to 4k users but never found repeatable revenue; 3 lessons.
draft:
After 3 years, I've made the hardest decision of my professional life: I'm shutting down Cartful.

We raised $1.1M. We grew to 4,000 users. We poured everything we had into this company. And yet, we never found repeatable revenue.

Writing this post is painful — but I owe it to everyone who believed in us to share what I learned.

Lesson 1: Users are not customers. We celebrated signups while avoiding the harder question: who will actually pay, and why?

Lesson 2: Repeatable revenue beats everything. One-off deals feel like traction. They're not. If you can't describe your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one.

Lesson 3: Runway is for learning, not surviving. We stretched our runway to stay alive instead of spending it to find the truth faster.

To our investors, our team, and our users: thank you. I'm sorry we couldn't get there.

Failure isn't the opposite of success. It's tuition.

On to the next chapter. 🙏

Unpopular opinion: networking events are mostly useless.

I used to attend every conference, every mixer, every "founder happy hour." I collected hundreds of business cards. Want to know how many clients came from all that networking?

Zero.

Meanwhile, my last 3 clients all came from the same place: writing online.

Here's why writing beats networking:

✍️ Scale — a conversation reaches one person; a post reaches thousands
✍️ Selection — the right people come to you, already pre-sold on how you think

Networking events optimize for feeling productive. Writing optimizes for being findable.

Now, I'm not saying relationships don't matter — they're everything. But the best relationships start when someone reads your ideas and thinks, "this person gets it."

Stop collecting business cards. Start publishing your thinking.

Your next client isn't at a conference. They're scrolling their feed, waiting to discover you.

brief: VC newsletter segment on vertical SaaS; thesis: AI makes small vertical markets viable; example: software for marinas, a $400M TAM.

draft:
This week, let's talk about vertical SaaS — and why we think the playbook is being rewritten in real time.

The old objection to vertical software was always market size. A niche industry might desperately need better tools, but if the TAM couldn't support a venture-scale outcome, investors passed. AI changes that math. When a small team can build, sell, and support software that previously required fifty people, small vertical markets suddenly become viable — and even attractive.

Take software for marinas: a $400M TAM that most funds would have ignored a decade ago. Today, an AI-native team can serve that market profitably at a fraction of the historical cost structure, own the core workflow end to end, and expand into payments, insurance, and adjacent services over time.

Our thesis is simple: the next generation of great vertical SaaS companies will be smaller teams attacking smaller markets — and capturing far more of them. If you're building in this space, we'd love to hear from you.

brief: LinkedIn-article-length piece (200 words) on AI in legal ops: contract review time down 60% at pilot firms; caution about hallucinated citations; mentions ABA guidance.
facts: Contract review time down 60% at pilot firms
draft:
AI is quietly transforming legal operations — and the numbers are getting hard to ignore.

At pilot firms deploying AI-assisted contract review, review time is down 60%. Work that once consumed days of associate attention now takes hours, freeing legal teams to focus on negotiation strategy and higher-value counsel. For legal ops leaders under pressure to do more with less, that kind of efficiency isn't a nice-to-have; it's a mandate.

But the story comes with an important caveat: hallucinated citations. AI tools can generate authorities that look entirely plausible and simply do not exist — and courts have shown little patience with filings that include them. Every AI-assisted output still needs qualified human review. No exceptions.

The profession's guardrails are taking shape, too. The ABA has issued guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI, emphasizing competence, confidentiality, and supervision. The message is clear: adopt the technology, but own the output.

The takeaway for legal teams? Start with high-volume, lower-risk workflows like contract review. Measure everything. Keep humans firmly in the loop. The firms that pair AI's speed with lawyers' judgment won't just cut costs — they'll redefine what legal service looks like.

What's your team's experience with AI in legal ops? I'd love to hear it in the comments.

brief: Thread: opener + 5 tweets of cold-email tips; key stats: 4-line emails, one CTA, 8% reply rate achieved; each tweet under 280 chars.
draft:
Cold email isn't dead — most people are just doing it wrong.

Last year I sent thousands of cold emails and hit an 8% reply rate.

Here are the 5 lessons that changed everything: 🧵

1/ Keep it to 4 lines. Seriously. Your prospect is scanning on their phone between meetings. Four lines is enough to say who you are, why you're relevant, and what you want. Anything longer gets archived.

2/ One CTA. Not two. Not three. One. Every additional ask cuts your response rate. "Worth a 15-min chat?" beats a menu of options every single time.

3/ Personalize the first line — but make it real. "Loved your post on X" only works if you actually read it. One genuine sentence beats five templated ones.

4/ Follow up. Most replies come from the 2nd or 3rd email, not the 1st. A polite bump is not annoying — it's how deals actually happen. Silence is not a no.

5/ Track everything: subject lines, send times, CTAs. I only hit an 8% reply rate after treating cold email like a system, not a lottery. Iterate weekly. That's the whole secret. If this helped, a repost on the first tweet goes a long way 🙏

brief: Thread: opener + 4 tweets on bootstrapping to $10k MRR in 19 months; started as a $49 one-time product; pivoted to subscriptions month 7.
draft:
19 months ago, I launched a $49 one-time product.

This week, we crossed $10k MRR. No funding, no team, no audience.

Here's the bootstrapped playbook, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ Start ugly. The first version was a $49 one-time purchase — no subscriptions, no dashboard, barely a landing page. It made a handful of sales, but more importantly, it proved people would pay. Validation first, polish later.

2/ Listen for the pivot. Customers kept coming back with the same recurring problem — and a one-time product couldn't serve it. In month 7, we pivoted to subscriptions. Revenue dipped for a few weeks. Then it compounded.

3/ Do things that don't scale. I onboarded every early customer personally, answered every support email, and asked every churned user why they left. Those conversations wrote our roadmap for us.

4/ Patience is the moat. 19 months to $10k MRR isn't a rocket ship — and that's the point. Slow, compounding, profitable growth beats hype every time. If you're bootstrapping right now: keep going. It adds up.
